title: Apolipoproteins: apoB, apoC-II/C-III, apoE and Type 3 Dysbetalipoproteinaemia
summary: Learn how lipoprotein particles are built, why one apoB per particle makes apoB a particle count, how apoC-II and apoC-III control lipoprotein lipase, how the apoE isoforms differ, and how dysbetalipoproteinaemia is actually proven in the lab.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 18 Hits 2 (apoB = particle number), 4 (type 3 dysbetalipoproteinaemia), 9 (apoE isoforms), 10 (apoB-48, apoC-II/apoC-III) and 16 (lipoprotein structure). Checked against Behbodikhah 2021, Shapiro 2017, Loving 2020, Kumari 2021, Wolska 2017 (read via a page-fetch tool), Mahley 2016, Heidemann 2022, Pallazola 2020 and Sampson 2022. Hit 4’s “equal cholesterol and TG elevation” is qualified (register flag rv-fd-lipid-pattern); Hit 10’s “apoC-II deficiency functionally mimics LPL deficiency” is qualified (register flag rv-apoc2-milder). The Endotext chapter on lipoproteins (NCBI Bookshelf) was blocked by a captcha and was not read. Not taught: the mRNA-editing position for apoB-48 (memory hook), PCSK9, CETP.

objectives: Describe the core and surface components of a lipoprotein particle.
Explain why plasma apoB reflects atherogenic particle number, and distinguish apoB-100 from apoB-48.
State the roles of apoC-II and apoC-III in lipoprotein lipase activity and of the apoE isoforms in remnant clearance.
Outline how familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia is recognised and confirmed in the laboratory.

scenes.title: Orange creases in the palms
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a 52-year-old man with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Standard lipid panel: total cholesterol 310 mg/dL, triglycerides 380 mg/dL — a non-specific mixed hyperlipidaemia. On examination, orange-yellow deposits sit in the creases of both palms. Question token: “Which apolipoprotein is broken?”

cues.text: An invented patient: a fifty-two-year-old man with obesity and type 2 diabetes. Cholesterol and triglycerides are both raised.
On examination, orange-yellow deposits line the creases of both palms.
The standard panel only says mixed hyperlipidaemia. Which apolipoprotein is broken?

scenes.title: Particle anatomy and apoB
scenes.altText: Schematic lipoprotein particle: a hydrophobic core of triglycerides and cholesteryl esters, wrapped in an amphipathic surface monolayer of phospholipids, free cholesterol and apolipoproteins. ApoB card: one apoB molecule per atherogenic particle, so plasma apoB counts particles. ApoB-100 (4536 amino acids) is made mainly in the liver and is the apoB of VLDL, IDL, LDL and Lp(a). ApoB-48 (the N-terminal 2152 amino acids) is made in the intestine and is found on chylomicrons and their remnants. LDL is the most abundant atherogenic lipoprotein in fasting blood.

cues.text: Every lipoprotein is built the same way. Triglycerides and cholesteryl esters fill a water-hating core.
Around it sits a single surface layer of amphipathic phospholipids, free cholesterol and apolipoproteins, the part that faces the plasma.
Each atherogenic particle carries exactly one apoB, so plasma apoB counts particles. LDL is the most abundant of them in fasting blood.
The liver makes full-length apoB-100 for VLDL, IDL and LDL. The intestine makes the shorter apoB-48, found only on chylomicrons and their remnants.

scenes.title: Switches and keys: apoC-II, apoC-III, apoE
scenes.altText: Lipolysis card: lipoprotein lipase (LPL) on the capillary surface hydrolyses triglyceride in chylomicrons and VLDL. ApoC-II is its essential cofactor; apoC-III inhibits LPL and also blocks hepatic uptake of remnants. Loss of function of LPL or apoC-II (or apoA-V, LMF1, GPIHBP1) causes familial chylomicronaemia syndrome; apoC-II deficiency is usually less severe and of later onset than LPL deficiency. ApoE card: ligand that clears VLDL, IDL and chylomicron remnants via LDL receptors. Isoforms differ at residues 112 and 158: E2 Cys/Cys, E3 Cys/Arg, E4 Arg/Arg. E2 binds the LDL receptor at about 2% of normal; E4 raises LDL and is the major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease.

cues.text: Lipoprotein lipase strips triglyceride from chylomicrons and VLDL. ApoC-II is its essential cofactor. ApoC-III holds it back, and also blocks the liver from taking up remnants.
Losing lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II causes familial chylomicronaemia syndrome. ApoC-II deficiency looks alike clinically, but is usually milder and starts later.
ApoE is the key that lets the liver clear remnants through LDL receptors. Its three isoforms differ at residues one-twelve and one-fifty-eight.
ApoE3 is the usual form. ApoE2 binds the receptor at only about two percent of normal. ApoE4 raises LDL and is the major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer disease.

scenes.title: Proving dysbetalipoproteinaemia
scenes.altText: Mechanism card: apoE2 cannot clear cholesterol-enriched remnants (β-VLDL), which accumulate. Genetics card: about 90% of familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia is ε2ε2, but only 10–15% of ε2ε2 people develop the phenotype, usually with a second hit (obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes; also hypothyroidism or oestrogen deficiency). Lab card: the standard panel shows only a non-specific mixed hyperlipidaemia (it can be predominantly TG or cholesterol); ultracentrifugation VLDL-C/total TG > 0.30 (mg/dL); broad-β band on agarose: specific but insensitive; apoB-based ratios when ultracentrifugation is unavailable. Formal diagnosis: phenotype plus a causal APOE genotype. Palmar crease xanthomas: pathognomonic but rare. Hook answer: apoE (likely E2/E2) plus diabetes and obesity.

cues.text: ApoE2 cannot clear cholesterol-enriched remnants, called beta-VLDL, so they pile up. About ninety percent of familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia is apoE2 homozygosity.

But only a minority of E2 homozygotes, about ten to fifteen percent in one review, ever develop it. A second hit is usually needed: obesity, insulin resistance or diabetes, and also hypothyroidism or low oestrogen.

The standard panel only shows a mixed pattern, sometimes mostly triglyceride or mostly cholesterol. Ultracentrifugation shows a VLDL-cholesterol to triglyceride ratio above zero point three. The broad-beta band is specific but insensitive, and apoB-based ratios help when ultracentrifugation is unavailable.
Diagnosis needs the phenotype plus a causal APOE genotype. Palmar crease xanthomas are pathognomonic but rare. Our patient: apoE, with diabetes and obesity as the second hit.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Type 3 always raises cholesterol and triglyceride equally” (✓ usually mixed, but can be predominantly TG or cholesterol; the standard panel cannot make the diagnosis); “ε2ε2 genotype = disease” (✓ only 10–15% of ε2ε2 express the phenotype); “LDL carries apoB-48” (✓ LDL carries apoB-100; apoB-48 is only on chylomicrons and remnants).

cues.text: Trap one: type 3 always raises cholesterol and triglyceride equally. No: it is usually mixed but can lean either way, and the standard panel cannot diagnose it.
Trap two: an E2 E2 genotype means the disease. No: only a minority of E2 homozygotes, roughly ten to fifteen percent, develop it.
Trap three: LDL carries apoB-48. No: LDL carries apoB-100. ApoB-48 stays on chylomicrons and their remnants.

props.title: ✗ “Type 3 = equal TC and TG rise.”
lines: ✓ Usually mixed, can lean either way

scenes.title: Plate, switch, key
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Every truck has ONE licence PLATE (apoB) — count plates to count trucks; B-48 plates are issued by the Bowel. C-II is the green SWITCH for lipase, C-III the red one. ApoE is the docking KEY: E2 is a bent key that only jams the lock when traffic is heavy.” Tokens: plate = apoB · switch = apoC-II/C-III · key = apoE. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: every truck has one licence plate, apoB, so counting plates counts trucks, and B-48 plates come from the bowel. ApoC-II is the green switch for lipase, apoC-III the red one. ApoE is the docking key, and E2 is a bent key that only jams the lock when traffic is heavy.
Where it breaks: apoC-III also blocks remnant uptake by the liver, too much apoC-II can also reduce lipolysis, and other APOE variants can cause dysbetalipoproteinaemia too.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “One apoB per particle · B-100 liver, B-48 intestine · apoC-II on, apoC-III off”, “apoE2 binds ~2% → remnants pile up only with a second hit · prove phenotype + genotype”.

cues.text: Each atherogenic particle carries one apoB, apoC-II switches lipoprotein lipase on while apoC-III holds it back, and apoE2, which barely binds the LDL receptor, causes dysbetalipoproteinaemia only when a second metabolic hit is added.

props.label: One apoB per particle · B-100 liver, B-48 gut · C-II on, C-III off
apoE2 ~2% binding → type 3 only with a second hit

explanation.what: Plain language: fat travels in blood inside tiny particles with an oily centre and a water-friendly skin. Proteins on the skin act as labels: apoB holds the particle together (one per particle), apoC-II and apoC-III turn the fat-clearing enzyme on and off, and apoE is the key that lets the liver take leftovers back. A faulty apoE key (E2) can let leftover particles pile up. Scientific terms: hydrophobic core, amphipathic surface monolayer, apoB-100, apoB-48, lipoprotein lipase (LPL), familial chylomicronaemia syndrome (FCS), apoE2/E3/E4, β-VLDL, familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia (type III hyperlipoproteinaemia), ultracentrifugation, VLDL-C/TG ratio, broad-β band.
explanation.why: Because each atherogenic particle carries one apoB, apoB measures particle number. LPL needs apoC-II, so losing either causes chylomicronaemia; apoC-III restrains LPL and remnant uptake. ApoE2 binds LDL receptors poorly, so remnant clearance is fragile; disease appears when a second hit (obesity, insulin resistance, diabetes, hypothyroidism, oestrogen deficiency) increases VLDL production or reduces receptors.
explanation.measure: ApoB-100 (4536 amino acids): liver; VLDL, IDL, LDL, Lp(a). ApoB-48 (N-terminal 2152 amino acids): intestine; chylomicrons and remnants. ApoE isoforms: residues 112/158 — E2 Cys/Cys, E3 Cys/Arg, E4 Arg/Arg; E2 ~2% receptor binding. Dysbetalipoproteinaemia: ~90% ε2ε2; low penetrance (10–15% in Heidemann 2022; under 5% in Pallazola 2020); ultracentrifugation VLDL-C/total TG > 0.30 (mass; 0.25–0.30 borderline); broad-β band specific but insensitive; apoB-based algorithms when ultracentrifugation is unavailable; formal diagnosis = phenotype + causal APOE genotype.
explanation.differs: apoB-100 (liver, LDL) vs apoB-48 (intestine, chylomicrons); apoC-II (LPL cofactor) vs apoC-III (LPL inhibitor); apoE2 (poor receptor binding, type 3) vs apoE4 (higher LDL, Alzheimer risk); LPL deficiency vs apoC-II deficiency (similar FCS, apoC-II usually milder and later).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: match apoB-48 to chylomicrons, apoC-II to LPL activation, apoE2/E2 to type 3 with palmar xanthomas and β-VLDL, and recognise that apoB counts particles; watch for “equal TC and TG” and “genotype = disease” overstatements.

comparisons.title: apoB-100 vs apoB-48
comparisons.distinguisher: Where it is made and which particle carries it.

comparisons.title: apoC-II vs apoC-III
comparisons.distinguisher: Turns triglyceride clearance on vs holds it back.

mnemonic.text: Every truck has ONE licence PLATE (apoB) — count plates to count trucks; B-48 plates come from the Bowel. C-II is the green SWITCH for lipase, C-III the red one. ApoE is the docking KEY: E2 is a bent key that only jams the lock when traffic is heavy.
mnemonic.explanation: Links apoB to particle number, apoC-II/C-III to LPL control, and apoE2 to low-penetrance remnant disease.
mnemonic.limitation: apoC-III also blocks hepatic remnant uptake; excess apoC-II can also reduce lipolysis; other APOE variants (and rarely hepatic lipase deficiency) can cause a type 3 phenotype.

analogyLimitations: Particle drawing is schematic; real particles carry many other proteins.
Lipid cut-offs for type 3 differ between ultracentrifugation and apoB-based methods.
takeaway: Each atherogenic particle carries one apoB, apoC-II switches lipoprotein lipase on while apoC-III holds it back, and apoE2, which barely binds the LDL receptor, causes dysbetalipoproteinaemia only when a second metabolic hit is added.

questions.stem: Which apolipoprotein is the essential cofactor of lipoprotein lipase, so that its loss of function causes familial chylomicronaemia syndrome?

options.rationale: Correct. ApoC-II is the essential LPL cofactor; biallelic loss of function causes FCS, usually milder and later in onset than LPL deficiency.
Incorrect. ApoC-III inhibits LPL; APOC3 variants that reduce it are associated with lower triglycerides.
Incorrect. ApoB-48 is the structural protein of chylomicrons, not an LPL cofactor.
Incorrect. ApoE4 is a receptor-binding isoform linked to higher LDL and Alzheimer risk.

questions.stem: Which statement about familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia (type III hyperlipoproteinaemia) is correct?

options.text: Most cases are apoE2 homozygotes, but only a minority of apoE2 homozygotes develop the disorder
options.rationale: Correct. About 90% of cases are ε2ε2, yet only a minority of ε2ε2 people express the phenotype (10–15% in one review, under 5% in another), usually with a second metabolic hit.

options.text: A standard lipid panel showing equal cholesterol and triglyceride rises is diagnostic
options.rationale: Incorrect. The standard panel often gives only a non-specific mixed pattern; ultracentrifugation or apoB-based methods plus APOE genotyping are needed.

options.text: ApoE4 binds the LDL receptor at about 2% of normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is apoE2; apoE3 and apoE4 bind the receptor with similar affinity.

options.text: A normal agarose electrophoresis without a broad-β band rules it out
options.rationale: Incorrect. The broad-β band is specific but has low sensitivity.

questions.stem: Why does plasma apoB concentration reflect the number of atherogenic lipoprotein particles?

options.text: Each VLDL, IDL, LDL and Lp(a) particle carries exactly one apoB molecule
options.rationale: Correct. The one-apoB-per-particle ratio makes apoB a direct particle count.

options.text: ApoB is carried mainly by HDL
options.rationale: Incorrect. HDL does not carry apoB; apoB is on atherogenic particles.

options.text: ApoB-48 is the apoB of LDL
options.rationale: Incorrect. LDL carries apoB-100; apoB-48 is on chylomicrons and their remnants.

options.text: ApoB sits in the hydrophobic core with the triglycerides
options.rationale: Incorrect. Apolipoproteins are on the surface monolayer; the core holds triglycerides and cholesteryl esters.

claims.text: Lipoprotein core (TG, CE) and amphipathic surface monolayer (phospholipids, free cholesterol, apolipoproteins).
One apoB per atherogenic particle; apoB as particle count; LDL most abundant atherogenic lipoprotein; apoB-100 vs apoB-48 origin and carriers.
ApoC-II essential LPL cofactor; apoC-III inhibits LPL and remnant uptake; FCS causes; apoC-II deficiency usually milder and later.
ApoE isoforms at residues 112/158; E2 ~2% receptor binding; E4 raises LDL and Alzheimer risk.
Dysbetalipoproteinaemia genetics, penetrance, second hits, lab criteria and xanthomas.
claims.note: Penetrance figures differ: Heidemann 2022 gives 10–15%, Pallazola 2020 “fewer than 5%”; the lesson uses Heidemann.

claims.text: ApoB-48 produced by mRNA editing at a specific codon (reviewer memory hook “position 6666”).
claims.note: No source read in this session describes the editing site; not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 18 Hit 4 presents type 3 as an “equal cholesterol and TG elevation” recognisable pattern. Heidemann 2022: usually a mixed hyperlipidaemia but it can be predominantly hypertriglyceridaemia or hypercholesterolaemia, the standard panel cannot detect the phenotype, and only 10–15% of ε2ε2 people express it; Sampson 2022: tubero-eruptive xanthomas are not specific (register flag rv-fd-lipid-pattern).

Ch. 18 Hit 10 says apoC-II deficiency functionally mimics LPL deficiency. Wolska 2017: clinical features are usually indistinguishable, but apoC-II deficiency is usually less severe with later onset than LPL deficiency (register flag rv-apoc2-milder).
